card.name: Juego de mani
card.era: Clearly by the 19th c. on Cuban sugar plantations; Kongo-Angola roots
card.tagline: Afro-Cuban combat dance, a Cuban cousin of capoeira.
card.profile: Juego de mani (also mani, baile de mani, or bambosa) is a combined martial art and dance developed by enslaved Africans in Cuba, with roots in Kongo-Angola (Central African) culture. Historically popular in Matanzas and Las Villas, it featured circling, competitive male dancing in a ring; practitioners are maniseros. The rhythm is set by drummers, using the music of Palo Monte. Techniques include low kicks, foot sweeps, punches, elbow and palm strikes; sticks and machetes were sometimes used. It influenced non-combative social dances such as rumba columbia (English Wikipedia; Capoeira History, citing Fernando Ortiz 1951).
card.insight: Scholars including Matthias Rohrig Assuncao note mani shares form and meaning with capoeira, supporting the view that African-derived combat games in the Americas shared common Kongo-Angola features (English Wikipedia).
